polar_bear_swim_day.label: Polar Bear Swim Day
polar_bear_swim_day.intro: On the first day of the year, brave souls run straight into ice-cold seas and lakes. A few seconds of shrieking, a lot of laughing — and a story to tell for the rest of the year.
funFacts: Around 60,000 people take part in the Dutch Nieuwjaarsduik every 1 January, a tradition running since 1960.
Since 1998 the Dutch swimmers have been easy to spot: sponsor Unox hands out orange winter hats.
Scotland has the Loony Dook in South Queensferry, where many participants plunge in fancy dress.

science_fiction_day.label: National Science Fiction Day
science_fiction_day.intro: A day for spaceships, time machines and impossible worlds. The date is the birthday Isaac Asimov picked for himself, so it doubles as a nod to one of the genre's most prolific authors.
funFacts: Asimov never knew his exact date of birth and simply declared 2 January his birthday.
The word 'robotics' was coined by Asimov in a short story published in 1941.
Mary Shelley's Frankenstein of 1818 is often described as the first science fiction novel.

festival_of_sleep_day.label: Festival of Sleep Day
festival_of_sleep_day.intro: After the marathon of parties and family visits comes the friendliest task of the year: sleep in. Curtains closed, blanket up, alarm off — napping is officially on the programme.
funFacts: We spend roughly a third of our lives asleep.
One sleep cycle lasts about 90 minutes and repeats four to six times a night.
Domestic cats sleep twelve to sixteen hours a day, spread across plenty of short naps.

spaghetti_day.label: National Spaghetti Day
spaghetti_day.intro: Long, thin and endlessly twirlable: today belongs to the most famous pasta shape in the world. Sauce optional, second helping expected.
funFacts: The name comes from the Italian word 'spago', meaning string or twine.
In 1957 the BBC programme Panorama fooled viewers with a report on the Swiss spaghetti harvest.
Italy leads the world in pasta consumption with roughly 23 kilograms per person per year.

bird_day.label: National Bird Day
bird_day.intro: Winter is the best time to watch birds: bare branches, busy feeders and plenty of visitors. A day for looking up and listening closely.
funFacts: Hummingbirds beat their wings up to 80 times per second, which is why they can hover on the spot.
Arctic terns migrate between the Arctic and the Antarctic and cover tens of thousands of kilometres a year.
Birds are living dinosaurs: they descend directly from small feathered theropods.

shortbread_day.label: National Shortbread Day
shortbread_day.intro: Three ingredients, one very good biscuit: Scottish shortbread is pure butter, sugar and flour. Crumbly, golden and made for a pot of tea.
funFacts: The classic recipe follows a 1-2-3 rule: one part sugar, two parts butter, three parts flour.
A round shortbread cut into wedges is traditionally called 'petticoat tails'.
Its ancestor was medieval twice-baked biscuit bread, which slowly gained more and more butter.

tempura_day.label: National Tempura Day
tempura_day.intro: Feather-light batter, hot oil, a little patience: tempura turns prawns, mushrooms and green beans into something crisp and golden.
funFacts: Portuguese missionaries brought the idea of battered deep-fried food to Japan in the 16th century.
The name is usually traced to the Latin 'tempora', the fasting days on which fish was eaten.
In old Edo, tempura was street food: sold on skewers at stalls and eaten standing up.

bubble_bath_day.label: National Bubble Bath Day
bubble_bath_day.intro: Hot water, a mountain of foam and nowhere to be: the bubble bath is the coziest way to survive January. Book and candle strictly optional.
funFacts: The skin of a soap bubble is only a few hundred nanometres thick, far thinner than a human hair.
Bubbles are round because a sphere encloses the most volume with the least surface.
Mr. Bubble, launched in the United States in 1961, turned foam baths into a children's classic.

balloon_ascension_day.label: Balloon Ascension Day
balloon_ascension_day.intro: The day remembers the first manned balloon flight over North America in 1793 — and is a fine excuse to look up whenever something colourful drifts across the sky.
funFacts: On 9 January 1793 Jean-Pierre Blanchard lifted off from a prison yard in Philadelphia.
George Washington watched the launch and handed Blanchard a letter asking for safe passage.
A hot air balloon rises simply because the heated air inside it is lighter than the air outside.

houseplant_appreciation_day.label: Houseplant Appreciation Day
houseplant_appreciation_day.intro: The Christmas tree is gone, the decorations are packed away — and the houseplants are still there. Time for water, a wipe of the leaves and a bit of praise.
funFacts: Why Monstera leaves develop holes is not fully settled. One hypothesis links them to variable light in the rainforest.
Victorian Britain caught 'pteridomania', a full-blown craze for collecting ferns.
In 1989 NASA tested houseplants in sealed chambers to see how well they filter the air.

milk_day.label: National Milk Day
milk_day.intro: A day for the most ordinary drink in the fridge — and for everything made from it: butter, cheese, yoghurt and the foam on top of a cappuccino.
funFacts: The date recalls the early days of home delivery, when milk first arrived in sealed glass bottles.
Most adults worldwide cannot digest lactose; tolerating it into adulthood is the exception.
It takes roughly twenty litres of milk to churn a single kilogram of butter.

marzipan_day.label: National Marzipan Day
marzipan_day.intro: Ground almonds and sugar, shaped into pigs, potatoes or plain little loaves: marzipan is the sweet that survives long after the holidays are over.
funFacts: Marzipan is essentially just almonds and sugar — the almond content decides the quality.
Lübecker Marzipan carries a protected geographical indication in the European Union.
Persipan looks the same but is made from apricot or peach kernels instead of almonds.

rubber_duck_day.label: National Rubber Ducky Day
rubber_duck_day.intro: Yellow, squeaky and unsinkable: the rubber duck is the smallest star in any bathroom. Today it gets the applause it has quietly earned for decades.
funFacts: In 1992 a container of bath toys went overboard in the Pacific; the floating ducks helped researchers map ocean currents.
Ernie's song 'Rubber Duckie' actually charted in the United States in 1970.
Artist Florentijn Hofman has toured harbours worldwide with rubber ducks several storeys high.

dress_up_your_pet_day.label: Dress Up Your Pet Day
dress_up_your_pet_day.intro: Scarf, bow tie or full dinosaur outfit: today pets are allowed a wardrobe. Rule number one — if the animal is not enjoying it, the photo is over.
funFacts: Pet lifestyle author Colleen Paige launched the day in 2009.
For short-haired breeds such as greyhounds a winter coat is not a costume but genuinely useful.
In the United States, Halloween outfits for pets are a market worth hundreds of millions of dollars.

hat_day.label: National Hat Day
hat_day.intro: Beanie, beret, bowler or a woolly hat with a pompom: in the middle of winter a hat is both practical and a statement. Today, wear the loudest one you own.
funFacts: The bowler hat was created in 1849 by London hatters Lock & Co. as sturdy headgear for gamekeepers.
The phrase 'mad as a hatter' points to the mercury once used in felting hats.
The Panama hat is woven in Ecuador and only picked up its name in transit.

nothing_day.label: National Nothing Day
nothing_day.intro: A day with nothing on the agenda: nothing to celebrate, nothing to commemorate, nothing to organise. Deliberately the emptiest square in the calendar.
funFacts: Columnist Harold Pullman Coffin proposed the non-event in 1972; it has been observed since 1973.
The point was a counterweight to the ever-growing flood of special days in the calendar.
The Dutch have a word for productive idling: 'niksen', doing nothing on purpose.

kid_inventors_day.label: Kid Inventors' Day
kid_inventors_day.intro: Some of the best everyday objects were dreamed up by children. The date is Benjamin Franklin's birthday — he built his first invention at the age of twelve.
funFacts: Benjamin Franklin, born 17 January 1706, carved wooden swim fins for his hands when he was twelve.
The ice lolly goes back to 11-year-old Frank Epperson, who left a drink with a stirrer outside overnight in 1905.
Chester Greenwood came up with earmuffs as a teenager and had them patented a few years later.

winnie_the_pooh_day.label: Winnie the Pooh Day
winnie_the_pooh_day.intro: The birthday of author A. A. Milne is celebrated as the day of his most famous creation: a bear of very little brain with an unlimited appetite for honey.
funFacts: A. A. Milne was born on 18 January 1882; his son Christopher Robin lent his name to the character.
Pooh is named after Winnipeg, a real black bear that lived at London Zoo.
The Latin edition 'Winnie ille Pu' made the New York Times bestseller list in 1960.

popcorn_day.label: National Popcorn Day
popcorn_day.intro: Sweet or salty, cinema or sofa: popcorn is the snack that makes noise before you even eat it. A whole day for the loudest corn in the kitchen.
funFacts: A kernel pops at around 180 °C, when the water inside turns to steam and blows the hull apart.
Popcorn remains several thousand years old have been found in caves in New Mexico.
Charles Cretors demonstrated a steam-powered popcorn machine at the 1893 Chicago World’s Fair.

cheese_lovers_day.label: National Cheese Lovers Day
cheese_lovers_day.intro: Soft, hard, mild or pungent: cheese is one of humanity's oldest foods. Today belongs to everyone who prefers to eat it straight off the board — bread optional.
funFacts: The oldest traces of cheesemaking sit in roughly 7,500-year-old clay sieves from Kuyavia in Poland.
The holes in Emmental are made by bacteria that release carbon dioxide while the cheese ripens.
France, Iceland, Finland, Denmark and Germany lead the table with around 25 kilos of cheese per person a year.

hugging_day.label: National Hugging Day
hugging_day.intro: One of the simplest ideas in the calendar: hug the people you like. In the middle of a grey January that is worth more than any gift.
funFacts: Kevin Zaborney came up with the day in 1986 in the small town of Caro, Michigan.
Hugging releases oxytocin, the hormone associated with closeness and calm.
Studies clock the average spontaneous hug at only about three seconds.

answer_your_cats_questions_day.label: Answer Your Cat's Questions Day
answer_your_cats_questions_day.intro: Cats stare, blink and clearly expect something. Today the rule is simple: answer out loud, in full sentences, and take the conversation seriously.
funFacts: Adult cats meow mainly at humans and hardly ever at each other.
A purr sits roughly between 25 and 150 hertz — cats also purr when they are unwell.
About thirty muscles move each ear, which is why cats can swivel them almost 180 degrees.

handwriting_day.label: National Handwriting Day
handwriting_day.intro: Keyboards are faster, but nothing beats a handwritten note. Today is for pens, paper and the pleasure of a properly looping signature.
funFacts: The date is the birthday of John Hancock, whose sweeping signature on the Declaration of Independence became legendary.
In American English 'John Hancock' is still a casual word for a signature.
No two hands write alike: experts compare pressure, slant and rhythm to tell them apart.

belly_laugh_day.label: Global Belly Laugh Day
belly_laugh_day.intro: A day dedicated to the kind of laugh that shakes your whole body. The instructions are refreshingly simple: throw your arms up and laugh out loud.
funFacts: The tradition is to laugh at 1:24 p.m. local time, arms raised, wherever you happen to be.
Laughter is contagious: in company people laugh far more often than when alone.
Rats squeak at ultrasonic frequencies when tickled — researchers read it as a form of laughter.

burns_night.label: Burns Night
burns_night.intro: Scotland celebrates its national poet Robert Burns with a supper, bagpipes and poetry read out loud. The haggis is not merely served — it is formally addressed.
funFacts: Robert Burns was born on 25 January 1759; friends held the first Burns Supper in his memory in 1801.
The haggis is piped into the room and greeted with the poem 'Address to a Haggis'.
'Auld Lang Syne', sung around the world at New Year, goes back to Burns.

peanut_brittle_day.label: National Peanut Brittle Day
peanut_brittle_day.intro: Caramel, peanuts, one loud crack: brittle is the least complicated sweet there is. It needs a saucepan, a bit of nerve and cold hands afterwards.
funFacts: Peanuts are not nuts at all but legumes, and they ripen underground.
A pinch of baking soda makes the hot caramel foam, which is what turns brittle light and crunchy.
Nut brittle exists worldwide: chikki in India, croccante in Italy, pasteli with sesame in Greece.

kazoo_day.label: National Kazoo Day
kazoo_day.intro: The kazoo needs no lessons, no talent and no tuning. You hum into it and a comically buzzing sound comes out — the most democratic instrument in the world.
funFacts: You do not blow a kazoo, you hum: a thin membrane turns the voice into that buzzing tone.
The Original American Kazoo Company in Eden, New York, has been pressing metal kazoos since 1916.
Because there is nothing to finger, the kazoo counts as one of the easiest instruments to learn.

puzzle_day.label: National Puzzle Day
puzzle_day.intro: Jigsaws, crosswords, riddles and brain teasers: a day for everything that keeps you happily stuck for an hour. Perfect timing for a dark January evening.
funFacts: Around 1760 London map seller John Spilsbury glued a map onto wood and sawed it apart — the first jigsaw puzzle.
The first crossword appeared in 1913 in the New York World, devised by Arthur Wynne.
The largest jigsaw puzzles on the market have well over 40,000 pieces.

croissant_day.label: National Croissant Day
croissant_day.intro: Crisp outside, airy inside and a trail of flakes on the table: the croissant is the best argument for getting up early. Today it counts as a full breakfast.
funFacts: The croissant descends from the Austrian Kipferl; Viennese baker August Zang brought it to Paris in 1839.
The dough is folded again and again so that dozens of thin layers of butter puff up in the oven.
Croissant au beurre means a butter croissant; the shape alone is not a reliable guide to the ingredients.

backwards_day.label: Backwards Day
backwards_day.intro: Jumper on back to front, dessert before soup, names read from the end: the last day of January flips the order of everything. It is a classic in American schools.
funFacts: Leonardo da Vinci wrote his notebooks in mirror writing, legible only when held up to a mirror.
In 2015 Aaron Yoder ran a mile backwards in 5:54.25, setting a Guinness World Record at the time.
Palindromes work in both directions: 'racecar' reads exactly the same forwards and backwards.
